text:
This lesson only has slides (no handouts). You can find them here.

The slides include a lot of additional information in hidden slides for you about things to notice about Dataflow and what students might try as they learn to use it.

Logging into CLUE: Students should be getting pretty comfortable logging into CLUE. However, this will be the first time they are running a different (new) lesson. Make sure they run lesson 1.2. If they run the wrong lesson (L1.1) they can just close the tab and run L1.2.

In this lesson, students will be introduced to Dataflow.

Right from the beginning, we want this to be very inquiry oriented: there isn't a single correct way to do make any particular program.

Throughout the lesson, students will be figuring out how to make progressively more complex programs

  • Initially, students will be making a program that subtracts two numbers
  • Then, students will figure out how to connect a demo gripper to their program
  • Finally, students will figure out how to make their program work automatically (without having to change a number or numbers each time you want to open/close the gripper)

In the end of the lesson, students will document what they have figured out, and their strategies for figuring out new ideas.

Key things students figure out about Dataflow:

  • Dataflow works by sending numbers through a system (roughly speaking from left to right, although practically blocks can be organized in lots of ways, visually)
  • You can click the little graph button on blocks to see a graph of what the block is outputting over time.
  • Programs are made by connecting blocks through "wires" between grey dots
  • The gripper translates numbers between 0-1 to percent closed (e.g., 0.1 --> 10% closed)

Major ideas & practices of the lesson:

  • There is not one "correct answer" in this unit (and in science/engineering/computing)
  • There are many ways to write programs that complete a certain task. Each way has advantages & disadvantages
  • Students typically won't be given step-by-step instructions for making programs work -- they need to document their thinking so they can remember what they did in the future and communicate it to others, and develop good strategies for figuring out new things
  • Systematicity is useful for figuring out what Dataflow blocks do
